claims.text: The mechanical behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys in high-temperature service is governed by the formation and evolution of a complex hierarchical microstructure.
The thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys in high-temperature service is governed by the formation and evolution of a complex hierarchical microstructure.
Atomistic or mesoscale simulations can predict and explain this microstructure-dependent behavior.
The proposed initial state is an undeformed refractory high-entropy alloy.
Alloy composition, temperature, and deformation conditions are proposed as controlled variables.
The applicable high-temperature regime is above 1000 degrees Celsius.
The relevant hierarchical microstructure includes grain boundaries, dislocations, and precipitates.
Diffusion contributes to formation and evolution of the microstructure at high temperature.
Recrystallization contributes to formation and evolution of the microstructure at high temperature.
Grain growth contributes to formation and evolution of the microstructure at high temperature.
The proposed microstructural evolution produces improved strength relative to traditional nickel-based or cobalt-based superalloys.
The proposed microstructural evolution produces improved creep resistance relative to traditional nickel-based or cobalt-based superalloys.
The proposed microstructural evolution reduces thermoelastic stress relative to traditional nickel-based or cobalt-based superalloys.
The hypothesis applies at deformation rates relevant to industrial applications.
A lack of significant correlation between microstructure and mechanical or thermoelastic behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
Behavior inconsistent with atomistic or mesoscale simulation predictions would falsify the hypothesis.
